Stochastic Block Models for Multipartite networks: principle

Principle and illustration on simulated data

team großBM

2026-11-24

Source: vignettes/MultipartiteNetwork_principle.qmd

1. Preliminaries

This vignette presents the multipartite stochastic block model and illustrates, on simulated data, the use of the functions sampleMultipartiteSBM and estimateMultipartiteSBM and of the methods accompanying the R6 class MultipartiteSBM_fit. An application to a real ecological network is given in the vignette Multipartite Stochastic Block Models (vignette("Multipartite_EcologicalNetwork", package = "sbm")).

The only package required for the analysis is sbm:

library(sbm)

2. Multipartite networks

Multipartite networks consist in the joint observation of several networks implying some common individuals. The individuals (or entities represented by nodes) at stake are partitioned into groups defined by their nature, for instance plants, pollinators and birds in an ecological network. In what follows, these groups are referred to as functional groups (they are the dimLabels of the networks in sbm).

A multipartite network is a collection of networks, each of them involving one or two functional groups:

  • a simple network represents the relations inside a functional group (adjacency matrix, directed or not),
  • a bipartite network represents the relations between the individuals of two functional groups (incidence matrix).

The networks may be binary or weighted, and different networks may have different types of weights.

3. Stochastic Block Models for multipartite networks

3.1 The model

Assume that SS functional groups are at stake, the functional group ss containing nsn_s nodes. We denote by ℰ\mathcal{E} the set of pairs of functional groups (s,s′)(s, s') for which a network Yss′Y^{ss'} is observed: Yijss′Y^{ss'}_{ij} is the interaction between node ii of functional group ss and node jj of functional group s′s'. If s≠s′s \neq s', Yss′Y^{ss'} is an incidence matrix (bipartite network); YssY^{ss} is an adjacency matrix, symmetric if the relation inside the functional group ss is not oriented.

The multipartite SBM

The nsn_s nodes of functional group ss are divided into QsQ_s blocks with proportions πs=(π1s,…,πQss)\pi^s = (\pi^s_1, \dots, \pi^s_{Q_s}), this clustering being encoded into the latent variables (Zis)i=1,…,ns(Z^s_i)_{i=1,\dots,n_s} such that Zis=qZ^s_i = q if node ii of functional group ss belongs to block qq. The clusterings of the functional groups are independent, and the interactions are driven by the blocks of the nodes: (Zis)i,s indep.ℙ(Zis=q)=πqs,(Yijss′)(s,s′)∈ℰ,i,j indep.∣(Zis)i,sYijss′∣Zis=q,Zjs′=r∼ℱss′(αqrss′),\begin{align*} (Z^s_i)_{i, s} \text{ indep.} \qquad & \mathbb{P}(Z^s_i = q) = \pi^s_q, \\ (Y^{ss'}_{ij})_{(s,s') \in \mathcal{E}, i, j} \text{ indep.} \mid (Z^s_i)_{i,s} \qquad & Y^{ss'}_{ij} \mid Z^s_i = q, Z^{s'}_j = r \sim \mathcal{F}_{ss'}(\alpha^{ss'}_{qr}), \end{align*} where ℱss′\mathcal{F}_{ss'} is Bernoulli, Poisson, Gaussian or Zero Inflated Gaussian, and may differ from one network to another.

The blocks of a functional group are thus defined by the patterns of connection of its nodes in all the networks it is involved in. This model is introduced in Bar-Hen et al. (2022).

3.2 Inference

The parameters are estimated with a variational version of the Expectation-Maximization algorithm, which also supplies the clustering of the nodes. The numbers of blocks (Qs)s=1,…,S(Q_s)_{s=1,\dots,S} are chosen with a penalized likelihood criterion (ICL), by a forward-backward exploration: starting from an initial clustering, blocks are split or merged, one functional group at a time, as long as the ICL increases.

By default, the initial clusterings are obtained by fitting a simple or bipartite SBM on each network separately (with the package blockmodels); all the combinations of these clusterings are used as starting points (option initBM = TRUE). An initial clustering can also be given by the user (option classifInit, see Section 7).

The networks may contain missing values (NA): the corresponding dyads are assumed to be missing at random and are ignored in the inference.

The inference is performed by the package GREMLINS.

4. Data simulation

We simulate a multipartite network involving 22 functional groups, A and B, of respective sizes nA=60n_A = 60 and nB=50n_B = 50, divided into 33 and 22 blocks.

nbNodes   <- c(60, 50)
blockProp <- list(c(0.16, 0.40, 0.44), c(0.3, 0.7)) # proportions of the blocks in each functional group

We observe 33 networks:

  • A-B: continuous weighted interactions (Gaussian),
  • B-B: binary directed interactions (Bernoulli),
  • A-A: counts, undirected (Poisson).

The architecture of the multipartite network is given by a matrix with one row per network, giving the indices of the functional groups in row and in column.

archiMultipartite <- rbind(c(1, 2), c(2, 2), c(1, 1))
model    <- c("gaussian", "bernoulli", "poisson")
directed <- c(NA, TRUE, FALSE) # NA for a bipartite network
C1 <- list(mean = matrix(c(6.1, 8.9, 6.6, 9.8, 2.6, 1.0), 3, 2),
           var  = matrix(c(1.6, 1.6, 1.8, 1.7, 2.3, 1.5), 3, 2))
C2 <- list(mean = matrix(c(0.7, 1.0, 0.4, 0.6), 2, 2))
m3 <- matrix(c(2.5, 2.6, 2.2, 2.2, 2.7, 3.0, 3.6, 3.5, 3.3), 3, 3)
C3 <- list(mean = 0.5 * (m3 + t(m3))) # symmetric, the network being undirected
connectParam <- list(C1, C2, C3)
mySampleMSBM <- sampleMultipartiteSBM(nbNodes, blockProp, archiMultipartite, connectParam,
                                      model, directed, dimLabels = c("A", "B"), seed = 2)
listSBM <- mySampleMSBM$listSBM
trueMemberships <- mySampleMSBM$memberships

listSBM is a list of networks, as defined by the function defineSBM. The data can be plotted with:

plotMyMultipartiteMatrix(listSBM)

5. Estimation with selection of the numbers of blocks

The numbers of blocks are chosen between the bounds given in nbBlocksRange, a list named with the functional groups (default: from 11 to 1010 blocks in each functional group).

myMSBM <- estimateMultipartiteSBM(listSBM, estimOptions = list(verbosity = 0, nbCores = 1))

The selected numbers of blocks and the agreement of the clusterings with the simulated ones (adjusted Rand index):

myMSBM$nbBlocks
#> A B 
#> 3 2
sapply(c("A", "B"), function(s) aricode::ARI(myMSBM$memberships[[s]], trueMemberships[[s]]))
#> A B 
#> 1 1

The estimated parameters:

myMSBM$blockProp
#> $A
#> [1] 0.1333333 0.3500000 0.5166667
#> 
#> $B
#> [1] 0.4 0.6
myMSBM$connectParam[[2]]
#> $mean
#>        [,1]      [,2]
#> [1,] 0.6625 0.3950000
#> [2,] 1.0000 0.6088889

All the models visited during the exploration are stored; $setModel() makes one of them the current model.

myMSBM$storedModels
#>   indexModel nbParams nbBlocks A nbBlocks B nbBlocks       ICL    loglik
#> 1          1       25          3          2        5 -5727.889 -5635.616
#> 2          2       17          2          2        4 -6247.506 -6184.561
#> 3          3       10          1          2        3 -7611.141 -7573.768
plot(myMSBM, type = "expected")

6. Estimation for given numbers of blocks

If the lower and upper bounds of nbBlocksRange are equal for all the functional groups, the parameters are estimated for these numbers of blocks, without model selection. The bounds may also be equal for some functional groups only.

myMSBM_fixed <- estimateMultipartiteSBM(listSBM,
  estimOptions = list(verbosity = 0, nbCores = 1, nbBlocksRange = list(A = c(3, 3), B = c(2, 2))))
myMSBM_fixed$nbBlocks
#> A B 
#> 3 2

7. Initial clustering

An initial clustering can be given with the option classifInit: a list with one vector of block labels per functional group, named with the functional groups. The search of the numbers of blocks then starts from this clustering (initBM is ignored). Here, we start from a clustering with a single block in A and 33 blocks in B.

set.seed(1)
myClassifInit <- list(A = rep(1, 60), B = sample(1:3, 50, replace = TRUE))
myMSBM_init <- estimateMultipartiteSBM(listSBM,
  estimOptions = list(verbosity = 0, nbCores = 1, classifInit = myClassifInit))
myMSBM_init$nbBlocks
#> A B 
#> 3 2
myMSBM_init$ICL
#> [1] -5727.889

With fixed numbers of blocks, classifInit must have these numbers of blocks: it is then the starting point of the variational EM algorithm.

8. Missing data

We remove 10%10\% of the dyads of each network, at random (symmetrically for the undirected network).

addNA <- function(net, prop) {
  Y <- net$networkData
  isNA <- matrix(runif(length(Y)) < prop, nrow(Y), ncol(Y))
  simple <- inherits(net, "SimpleSBM_fit")
  if (simple && !net$directed) isNA <- isNA | t(isNA)
  Y[isNA] <- NA
  defineSBM(Y, net$modelName, type = ifelse(simple, "simple", "bipartite"),
            directed = net$directed, dimLabels = net$dimLabels)
}
set.seed(3)
listSBM_NA <- lapply(listSBM, addNA, prop = 0.1)
myMSBM_NA <- estimateMultipartiteSBM(listSBM_NA, estimOptions = list(verbosity = 0, nbCores = 1))
myMSBM_NA$nbBlocks
#> A B 
#> 3 2
sapply(c("A", "B"), function(s) aricode::ARI(myMSBM_NA$memberships[[s]], trueMemberships[[s]]))
#> A B 
#> 1 1

The method predict gives the expected value of each dyad, which can be used to predict the missing ones. For the binary network B-B, the predicted probabilities of the missing dyads are higher when there is actually an edge:

pred <- myMSBM_NA$predict()
missingBB <- is.na(listSBM_NA[[2]]$networkData)
tapply(pred[[2]][missingBB], listSBM[[2]]$networkData[missingBB], mean)
#>         0         1 
#> 0.5315599 0.6906959

9. Parallel computing

The variational EM runs are parallelized with the package future. If no plan has been chosen, a multisession plan with nbCores workers (option of estimOptions, 22 by default) is used during the estimation. Another plan can be set before the call:

future::plan(future::multisession, workers = 4)
myMSBM <- estimateMultipartiteSBM(listSBM)
future::plan(future::sequential)

References

Bar-Hen, Avner, Pierre Barbillon, and Sophie Donnet. 2022. “Block Models for Generalized Multipartite Networks: Applications in Ecology and Ethnobiology.” Statistical Modelling 22 (4): 273–96. https://doi.org/10.1177/1471082X20963254.
